Submitted by u/CS_Survivor_99:
If you are entering your sophomore or junior year, brace yourself for the upper-level CS core classes. The estimated weekly workload for classes like Systems Programming and Algorithms is easily 12 to 15 hours, mostly spent staring at compiler errors or debugging segmentation faults in the lab. 

The coding projects are heavily weighted—often accounting for 50% of your final grade. A lot of people ask if you can skip lectures since the slide decks are posted online. The short answer is absolutely not. Professors frequently live-code exam-relevant algorithms right on the whiteboard that are completely missing from the official slides. If you don't show up to take notes on those edge cases, you will bomb the coding practicals. Start the projects the day they drop on Tuesday; if you wait until the weekend, you're toast.

Submitted by u/BizBro_2026:
Does the business school strictly enforce a grading curve, or is it a myth? I'm sitting at an 88% in Finance and panicking about my GPA.

Comments:
u/WallStreetBound: Yes, the business school strictly enforces a target GPA curve across all core undergraduate classes—typically capping the average section GPA at a 3.0. How individual professors handle it varies completely. 
u/AccountingKing: Exactly. While some macroeconomics professors will apply a generous upward curve to save the class if the midterm average was a 55%, accounting and finance professors are notorious for doing the opposite. They will strictly cap the total number of 'A' grades allowed per section to stay compliant with the curve, meaning even if you earn a 92% raw score, you could get bumped down to a B+ if too many students scored higher than you.

Blog Post: The Hidden Gems of Campus Faculty
When looking for electives, students often flock to giant lecture halls, but the real secret to maintaining your GPA is hunting down passionate, highly-rated professors teaching niche or under-enrolled subjects.

Professor Evelyn Thorne in the Anthropology department is a prime example. She teaches "History of Myth and Magic," an under-enrolled course that students rave about. Her teaching style is entirely conversational, and she stands out because she evaluates students through creative multimedia projects instead of traditional exams. Similarly, Dr. Alan Cross in Linguistics makes complex syntax rules incredibly accessible and sets an incredibly low-stress pacing where homework is rarely assigned.

Can we do a definitive head-to-head comparison of Jones vs Williams for CHEM 103? I need to register tomorrow morning.

Top Voted Breakdown:
- Exam Structure: Professor Jones uses standard multiple-choice exams that are entirely based on memorizing the lecture slides. Professor Williams, on the other hand, includes tricky short-answer conceptual questions and heavily weights the hidden footnotes in the textbook readings.
- Workload: Jones gives optional practice sets. Williams assigns mandatory weekly homework portfolios that take hours.
- Verdict: Take Jones if you want an easier path to an A; take Williams only if you actually need to learn the material deeply for the MCAT.

Submitted by u/FreshmanGuide:
Introductory writing seminars are a complete roll of the dice depending on which graduate Teaching Assistant (TA) you pull. While the official curriculum is identical, the actual grading rigor and weekly reading assignments vary wildly. 

TA Sarah's section requires three drafts per essay with intensive line-by-line feedback, whereas TA Mark's section is mostly graded on completion but has mandatory lecture attendance. If you miss more than two writing workshops in Mark's section, your participation grade drops by a full letter. Treat the syllabus as a baseline, but use the first week to gauge your TA's individual grading quirks.
